extracted.intended_audience: government attorneys and officials handling federal land acquisition, cessions of jurisdiction, and military reservation legal issues
extracted.subtask_description: Legal rules and standards for (1) when and how a State must consent or cede jurisdiction to the United States over lands acquired for public purposes, and (2) the legal effects of such cessions (exclusive vs. concurrent jurisdiction), including implications for taxation, criminal/civil process, appropriations (sec. 355 R.S.), rights of way, and application of State and Territorial laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of State consent for purchases
rubrics_metrics.description: A State may give consent by a single general act, prospective in terms, and covering all cases of future purchases by the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Texas legislature act of Apr. 4, 1871 was regarded as such; see Attorney General opinions cited. This permits broad future purchases without separate special acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of reservation to 'serve process' (concurrent jurisdiction reservation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reservation by the State of the right to execute process lawfully issued under its authority within and upon the sites may properly be regarded as reserving merely the right to serve process within the lands for acts done and crimes committed without the same, so as to prevent them from becoming an asylum for fugitives from justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When language reserves only service of process, the cession may be accepted as vesting exclusive jurisdiction in the United States. Cases: R. 142, 567 (Apr. 3, 1880); P. 27, 132 (Oct. 1888).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction language may defeat exclusive jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a State statute in consenting to purchase and ceding jurisdiction adds that jurisdiction shall be exercised 'concurrently with' the State, this qualification may be more than a mere reservation and inconsistent with a grant of exclusive jurisdiction to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such qualification can make it doubtful whether Federal officials (e.g., Secretary of War) may lawfully expend appropriations for erection of public buildings on the land. See R. 41, Feb. 1880.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive legislation equals exclusive jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive legislation and exclusive jurisdiction mean the same thing; a State reservation of concurrent jurisdiction is valid only insofar as it is not repugnant to the exclusive jurisdiction of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an act provided 'exclusive legislation and concurrent jurisdiction together with the State' the practical effect of the reservation was limited to service of civil and criminal process to prevent sanctuary for fugitives. Cases: R.50, 255 (May 1886); C.1581, July 1895.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the term 'purchase' in statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'purchase' as used in statutes has been construed as embracing all forms of acquiring title (including condemnation) except descent; but generally 'purchase' is used to mean acquisition by contract between the parties, without governmental interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court in Kohl v. U.S. noted that 'purchase' might technically include condemnation but ordinarily means contract acquisition. Where title was acquired by condemnation, a special act of cession of jurisdiction was advised. See P. 50, 474 (Dec. 1891).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special cession needed when land acquired by condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: When land is acquired by the United States by condemnation in exercise of eminent domain, obtain a special act of cession of jurisdiction from the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advised because 'purchase' in common statutory usage may not encompass condemnation acquisitions for purposes of the constitutional and statutory consent requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutes of consent are prospective unless clearly retrospective
rubrics_metrics.description: A statute consenting to purchase is not to be construed as retrospective unless its language clearly shows that it was so intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Louisiana general statute of 1891 consenting to purchases was prospective and did not apply to earlier purchases (Jackson Barracks). See R.45, 436 (Sept. 1882); L.50, 95 (Mar. 1886).

rubrics_metrics.name: State water laws not operative on reservations with exclusive jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws regulating use of stream water for irrigation are not operative on a military reservation over which the United States has exclusive jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties downstream outside the reservation have no legal rights under State law in waters while within the reservation; commanding officer should regulate use to avoid unnecessary waste. See C.2453 (July & Sept. 1896).

rubrics_metrics.name: State labor/compensation laws not apply on ceded reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws (e.g., employer insurance of workmen) do not extend over military reservations where jurisdiction has been ceded to the United States, except as to service of process reserved by the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York law Feb. 17, 1909 held not operative over West Point reservation where jurisdiction ceded. C.20947 (Oct. 12, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of cession: withdrawal from State political/legal jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where consent to purchase has been given or exclusive jurisdiction ceded, the land is no longer part of the State politically or legally; no State taxes can be imposed and inhabitants are withdrawn from State civil and criminal jurisdiction (except as reserved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such persons also lose certain state citizenship privileges (e.g., voting, public schools). Cases: R.49,187 (July 1885); R.21,567 (July 1866); C.3521 (Sept. 1897).

rubrics_metrics.name: State authorities' powers curtailed on ceded reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive jurisdiction withdraws territory and its inhabitants from all control of State authorities; State officials lack authority to perform functions (e.g., coroners holding inquests) within ceded territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local public health boards may not apply quarantine within reservations as a matter of right but may be permitted by comity after consultation with military authorities. See P.36,143 (Oct. 1889); C.17372 (Jan. 16, 1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of cession on public highways within reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the government acquires title to lands on both sides of a public roadway and the State ceded exclusive jurisdiction over the reservation, the cession cedes political jurisdiction over that portion of the roadway within the reservation and State authority over it ceases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The United States (local military authorities under Secretary of War orders) may close the roadway if necessary for reservation use. C.3565 (Oct. 13, 1897); O.14715 (May 12, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of property/effects found on reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: If jurisdiction has not been ceded, effects found on reservation should be turned over to the county sheriff; if jurisdiction has been ceded, unidentified property found on reservation may be deposited in the U.S. Treasury as escheated property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fort Dade (no cession) — sheriff; Fort Mellen (cession) — deposit in Treasury. C.11073 (Jan. 27, 1902); C.23692 (Aug. 4, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration of estates for persons dying on ceded reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where exclusive jurisdiction has been ceded, State courts lack authority to administer effects on the reservation unless the domicile is in the State; in practice, effects may be removed outside the reservation for turnover to administrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advised to take effects outside the reservation to be within State jurisdiction if necessary. O.16153 (Apr. 8, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: No State warrants/arrests within unconditionally exclusive reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the jurisdiction of the United States over any military reservation is unconditionally exclusive, no State official can legally serve a warrant upon an officer or soldier within the limits of such reservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only process issued from U.S. courts can be executed on such lands unless the State reserved the right to serve process in specified classes of cases. R.31,567 (July 1866); many subsequent opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of State process depends on sovereignty over soil
rubrics_metrics.description: Legality of service at a military post of process issued in a State court depends on whether sovereignty of the soil resides wholly in the United States or is shared by the State government; where exclusive jurisdiction has been ceded, State process generally cannot be served except in reserved cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no cession exists, State process and court jurisdiction operate as elsewhere in the State. See R.16,514 (Aug. 1865); R.21,567 (July 1866).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'other public building of any kind whatever' in sec. 355 R.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase includes structures such as viaducts and observation towers for which appropriations were made; cession of jurisdiction is therefore requested before appropriations can lawfully be expended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: P.43,454 (Nov. 1890); opinion treating Washington Aqueduct land within sec.355; many Attorney General opinions requiring cession before expenditures. See list of C. and O. opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to obtain cession for park purposes under sec. 355
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of section 355 R.S., cession of jurisdiction would be required where land is purchased for park purposes; apart from the statute, cession might be unnecessary or undesirable because State jurisdiction preserves convenient fora for trial of offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: C.13817 (Dec. 19, 1902) advised cession per sec.355 but noted practical considerations if statute absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 355 prohibits expenditure before State consent but does not preclude purchase
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 355 in prohibiting expenditure of public money upon lands purchased for specified purposes before State consent does not preclude the mere purchase itself; title may be acquired absent such consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution and sec.355 do not preclude acquisition of title; appropriations for improvements, however, require consent. See P.63,1 (Dec. 1893); P.64,330 (Apr. 1894).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for cession of jurisdiction over submerged lands beyond low-water mark
rubrics_metrics.description: Where title is limited to the line of ordinary low-water mark, a cession of jurisdiction over necessary soil under the water beyond low-water mark should be obtained from the State before an appropriation for construction (e.g., iron pier) is expended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied at Fort Monroe in view of secs. 355 and 4661 R.S.; see R.53,328 (Apr. 1887).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operation of State municipal laws and criminal laws on ceded reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: When political jurisdiction passes, municipal laws continue in force until abrogated by the new sovereign; in reservations within States, State laws other than criminal continue operative until changed by Congress, while State criminal laws are superseded by U.S. criminal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial reservations differ: Presidential reservation has no effect on Territorial laws unless modified by Congress. Cases: C.16691 (Sept. 10, 1902); C.19855 (June 4, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of sec. 5391 re: punishments by State laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5391 provides that offenses committed in places ceded shall be visited with same punishment as provided by State laws 'now in force', but the provision is limited to the laws of the several States in force at the time of enactment (1866) and thus is inoperative for States admitted after 1866.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this limitation, modification or reenactment of the provision is recommended rather than delegating congressional power to States. See P.57,458 (Feb. 1893); subsequent cases in Montana and Colorado.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial courts' power to issue process for officers/soldiers on posts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a military post is situated in a Territory, Territorial courts (creatures of Congress) are authorized to issue process for arrest of officers or soldiers and to proceed in civil actions or seizures not specially exempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comity suggests seeking permission from commanding officer to enter posts for service, but officers should not obstruct due service. See R.28,1 (July 1868); C.11141 (Aug. 21, 1901).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local municipal authority excluded from military reservations without statute
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of statute directly or by implication extending local government powers over a military reservation/post (e.g., District of Columbia arsenal), local health officers have no authority to enter and abate nuisances without consent of the military commander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public buildings and grounds of the United States are excepted from District government charge; reservations are governed by military orders/regulations. See R.42,270 (May 1879); C.17372 (Jan. 16, 1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting and conveyance of rights-of-way and municipal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A vesting of a right-of-way in the United States gives control to keep the way open and insure its continued use; municipalities cannot convey rights-of-way from laid-out streets unless the legislature has delegated such authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appropriation for constructing a road through a city street to a national cemetery could not be expended on a right-of-way granted by city ordinance where the legislature had not delegated authority. See P.30,45 (Jan. 1889); P.54-45 (July 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War's inability to grant permanent rights-of-way without congressional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Without express authority from Congress, the Secretary of War cannot grant to railway companies permanent rights-of-way over United States lands under his control, though he may grant revocable licenses to lay and maintain railway tracks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary has frequently used revocable licenses in practice, but permanent grants require Congressional authorization. (VI B and related opinions.)
